lessons.title: Scenes, Cameras, and Renderers
lessons.content:
# Scenes, Cameras, and Renderers

A basic Three.js application needs three core parts: a scene, a camera, and a renderer.

### Responsibilities
- The `Scene` holds objects, lights, and environment data.
- The `Camera` defines the viewpoint.
- The `Renderer` draws the scene to a canvas.

### Mental model
If the scene is the stage and objects are actors, the camera is the audience perspective and the renderer is what actually paints the frame.

lessons.title: Meshes, Geometry, and Materials
lessons.content:
# Meshes, Geometry, and Materials

Visible 3D objects are usually meshes composed of geometry plus a material.

### Examples
- Geometry defines shape such as a box, sphere, or plane.
- Material defines how that shape looks under light.
- A mesh combines both and can then be positioned, rotated, or scaled.

### Practical rule
Start with simple primitives while building behavior. Fancy models and shaders should come after interaction and scene structure are stable.

lessons.title: Animation Loop Basics
lessons.content:
# Animation Loop Basics

Three.js scenes that move or respond to input usually render inside an animation loop.

### Typical flow
1. Update object state.
2. Handle controls or physics.
3. Render the scene.
4. Request the next frame.

### Performance note
Only do the work needed for each frame. Heavy allocations or repeated scene reconstruction inside the loop will quickly hurt frame rate.

lessons.title: Lighting and Shadows
lessons.content:
# Lighting and Shadows

Lights make materials readable and help convey depth.

### Common light types
- Ambient light for base visibility
- Directional light for sun-like lighting
- Point light for localized sources
- Hemisphere light for simple sky/ground balance

### Practical tip
Enable shadows selectively. They improve realism, but they also increase rendering cost.

lessons.title: Loading Models and Textures
lessons.content:
# Loading Models and Textures

Three.js supports external assets such as GLTF models, images, and environment maps.

### Key loaders
- `GLTFLoader` for modern model pipelines
- `TextureLoader` for image textures
- `CubeTextureLoader` for skyboxes and environment reflections

### Engineering rule
Treat asset loading as async work with error states and fallbacks. Production scenes should not assume every file loads instantly or successfully.

lessons.title: User Interaction and Raycasting
lessons.content:
# User Interaction and Raycasting

Raycasting lets you detect which object a pointer or click intersects in 3D space.

### Typical uses
- Selecting objects
- Hover highlights
- Triggering labels or tooltips
- Simple scene editors or configurators

### Design note
Keep interaction layers clear. Not every mesh should be clickable, and invisible helper objects can simplify hit testing.

lessons.title: Responsive Scenes and Resize Handling
lessons.content:
# Responsive Scenes and Resize Handling

A Three.js app should react to viewport changes so the canvas stays sharp and correctly proportioned.

### Resize checklist
- Update camera aspect ratio.
- Call `camera.updateProjectionMatrix()`.
- Resize the renderer.
- Consider pixel ratio limits for performance.

### Mobile note
Rendering at full device pixel ratio on every device can be expensive. Clamp pixel ratio when performance matters.

lessons.title: Performance Profiling
lessons.content:
# Performance Profiling

Three.js performance depends on draw calls, texture sizes, geometry complexity, and per-frame work.

### Common improvements
- Reuse geometry and materials.
- Reduce unnecessary lights and shadows.
- Avoid large transparent layers when possible.
- Dispose of objects you no longer need.

### Review habit
Measure before and after changes. Performance work without measurement often just moves cost around.

lessons.title: Integrating Three.js into Web Apps
lessons.content:
# Integrating Three.js into Web Apps

Three.js often lives inside a larger React, Next.js, or vanilla web application.

### Integration concerns
- Mount and clean up canvas resources correctly.
- Keep scene setup separate from UI state when possible.
- Destroy event listeners, controls, and WebGL resources on teardown.

### Engineering rule
Memory leaks in WebGL apps are easy to miss. Always plan cleanup as part of the first implementation, not as a later fix.
